title: Coil-built narrow bottle vase in air-dry clay
subtitle: A tall narrow-necked vase built from coils, suitable for dried flowers
excerpt: A tall narrow-necked bottle vase built from coils of air-dry clay. The narrow neck means the vase holds a stem upright without needing water, making it suitable for dried flowers and grasses without any waterproofing. Coil building allows the tall form without a wheel or kiln.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Coil-building methods referenced from Encyclopedia Britannica 11th edition (1911) pottery entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rope of clay rolled between the palms, used as the building unit in coil construction
Clay diluted with water to a paste consistency, used as an adhesive for joining coils
The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is firm enough to support further coil building without collapsing
Fully air-dried and unfired; the final stage before sealing

content.text: A narrow-necked bottle vase in coil-built air-dry clay is a slower build than a pinch pot but can reach 20 to 25 cm tall without a kiln or wheel. The narrowing neck is achieved by placing each successive
coil
slightly inward at the top and allowing the form to firm up between sessions. No kiln is needed: the vase dries at room temperature over several days and is suitable for dried flowers once sealed.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay thinned with water)

content.text: Building the base
Roll a flat disc of clay about 10 cm in diameter and 8 mm thick. This is the base of the vase. Press the underside flat on the work surface.
Score the top edge of the base in a cross-hatch pattern and brush
slip
over it. Roll a coil about 10 mm in diameter and press it onto the slipped edge, working around the perimeter. Blend the join inward and outward with a finger.

Add further coils, one at a time, scoring and slipping each join before placing the next. Keep the coils the same diameter (about 10 mm) for the first 8 to 10 rows as the vase body widens gently outward.
Smooth the outer surface with a damp wooden rib every 3 to 4 coils to prevent the walls cracking outward under their own weight. Leave the interior unsmoothed for now.
Allow to reach leather-hard between sessions
Build 5 to 6 coils at a time, then cover the piece with a loose plastic bag and allow it to reach
leather-hard

before adding more. This keeps the lower walls firm enough to support the weight of new coils without the vase slumping outward. Each session takes around 45 minutes; the wait between sessions is 1 to 2 hours.
Narrowing the neck

Once the vase has reached its widest point (around 12 to 14 cm), begin placing each new coil very slightly inside the previous one to start the inward taper. Reduce the coil diameter from 10 mm to 8 mm as the shoulder narrows.
Continue narrowing until the opening reaches 4 to 5 cm in diameter at the top of the shoulder.
Build the neck upward from the shoulder with 6 mm coils, keeping them vertical so the neck does not flare. Finish the rim with a slightly thickened final coil smoothed to a clean edge.
Final smoothing and drying
Smooth the outer surface fully with a damp rib and sponge. Allow the vase to reach
bone-dry
over three to five days. Do not rush drying: the thick base dries much slower than the narrow neck. Cover the neck loosely to slow its drying relative to the body.
Finishing

Apply two coats of PVA to all outer surfaces. Once dry, paint or leave natural. A natural linen-coloured vase reads well with dried grasses and seed heads. The inside does not need painting. Do not fill with water: air-dry clay is not waterproof even when sealed with PVA.
Variations
Use paper-clay air-dry for a stronger body that is less likely to crack at the shoulder transition.
Add a textured surface by pressing a rope or lace strip against the coil surface before smoothing.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Walls slump outward as building progresses
items.cause: Too many coils added before the previous session was firm enough
items.fix: Allow the lower walls to reach leather-hard before adding more coils. Build in shorter sessions of 4 to 5 coils with rests between

items.problem: Neck cracks at the shoulder transition during drying
items.cause: The shoulder clay and neck clay dried at different rates, creating stress
items.fix: Cover the upper part of the vase with a damp cloth during the first 24 hours to even out the drying rate. Fill hairline cracks with fresh slip and allow to re-dry slowly

items.problem: Coil joins remain visible on the outer surface
items.cause: The rib was not used often enough during building to blend the joins
items.fix: Wet the surface very slightly and rub joins with a finger. At leather-hard, rub with a damp metal rib to close the joins before the final drying
